analysis.one_liner: Adds 20 years to every copyright, including works that were about to become free for anyone to use.
analysis.headline: Congress extended copyright terms by 20 years—retroactively covering existing works—and President Clinton signed it on October 27, 1998, after the Senate passed it by unanimous consent and the House by voice vote with no recorded opposition.
analysis.plain_summary: The law stretches copyright from the author's life plus 50 years to life plus 70, and for works made for hire from 75/100 years to 95/120 years. It also reaches back in time: any copyright then in its renewal term was stretched to 95 years from when it was first secured, and recordings fixed before 1972 stay protected until 2067 [S2] [S4]. The practical effect is that a huge body of books, films, songs, and cartoons that were on schedule to enter the public domain—and become free for anyone to copy, reprint, or remix—stayed locked up for 20 more years. A second title exempts small restaurants and bars from paying licensing fees for playing radio and TV music [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Copyright owners of works already in existence—especially large film studios, record labels, music publishers, and book publishers—get up to 20 more years of exclusive revenue on catalogs they already own, with no new creative effort required. Individual creators and their heirs gain expanded rights to terminate old transfers and reclaim rights from publishers [S2] [S3]. Small restaurants, bars, and shops gain an exemption from music licensing fees for playing radio or TV broadcasts within size and speaker limits [S3] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Studios, record labels, publishers, and authors' heirs

how_it_helps.text: Extends copyright in works created on or after 1978 to life of the author plus 70 years (up from 50), and works made for hire to 95 years from publication or 120 from creation (up from 75/100) [S2] [S4].

Retroactively extends copyrights then in their renewal term to 95 years from the original grant, and stretches protection for pre-1972 sound recordings under state law to February 15, 2067 [S2] [S3] [S4].
Restores and extends termination rights so authors or their heirs can reclaim copyrights they transferred decades earlier, including grants whose termination window had already expired [S2] [S4].

Exempts restaurants, bars, and small shops from copyright infringement for playing radio and TV broadcasts within square-footage and speaker limits, and lets small proprietors challenge performing-rights-society rates in court [S3] [S4].

Allows libraries and archives to reproduce works in their final 20 years of copyright for preservation, scholarship, or research—though only when the work has no normal commercial exploitation and copies are unavailable at a reasonable price [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who reads, watches, performs, or builds on older creative works. Twenty years' worth of books, films, songs, and artwork that would have entered the public domain instead remain under exclusive control, so publishers, theaters, schools, libraries, and independent creators must keep paying license fees or go without. The public-domain pipeline is pushed back for a generation.

drawbacks.text: The extension is retroactive: copyrights already in their renewal term were stretched to 95 years from the original grant, granting owners two more decades of revenue on works that were already created and already near the end of their terms [S2] [S4].

The library exemption is narrow: it applies only during a work's final 20 years of copyright, only to the library's own preservation or research use, and not to any subsequent use by the public [S3] [S4].
Title II exempts many restaurants, bars, and retail shops from paying for the music they play, which shrinks the royalties songwriters and music publishers collect from those venues [S3] [S4].
The 'sense of Congress' asking studios to negotiate a fund sharing extended royalties with screenwriters, directors, and performers is non-binding and carries no enforcement [S3] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had real sweeteners—termination rights for authors' heirs, a licensing break for small bars and restaurants, and a limited library preservation exemption—but its core is a 20-year retroactive extension of existing copyrights. That gives rights holders decades of extra exclusive revenue on works already made, while the public waits another generation for those works to become free. An honest supporter would concede that retroactive extensions offer no new creative incentive; the cost falls entirely on access to culture.

outcome.mechanism: It slipped through with essentially no friction: the Senate passed it by unanimous consent on October 7, 1998, the House passed it the same day by voice vote under a fast-track procedure, and the President signed it three weeks later.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on March 20, 1997, and it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee for over a year [S6].
On October 7, 1998, the committee was discharged and the Senate passed the bill with an amendment by unanimous consent—no roll-call, no recorded dissent [S6].
The same day, the House took it up under 'suspension of the rules,' a fast-track procedure reserved for noncontroversial bills, and passed it by voice vote [S6].
The President signed it on October 27, 1998, making it Public Law 105-298 [S6] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Film studios, record labels, music publishers, and other owners of existing catalogs are better off—they received up to 20 more years of exclusive revenue on works already created, many of which were months to years from becoming free for anyone to use. Small bars and restaurants also gained from the music licensing exemption.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no opposition at all: 11 cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 7 Republicans, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and the House passed it by voice vote with no roll call and no recorded dissents [S5] [S6].

industries.industry: Film studios and major media companies
industries.note: They received 20 extra years of exclusive control over existing films, including 1920s-era works about to enter the public domain. The public's gain would have been free access to those works; instead that access is postponed.

Pre-1972 sound recordings stay protected under state law until 2067, and old song copyrights in their renewal term were stretched to 95 years. Ordinary listeners and cover artists keep paying for works nearly a century old.

industries.industry: Small restaurants, bars, and retail shops
industries.note: Title II exempts them from infringement claims for playing radio and TV broadcasts within size and speaker limits, sparing small businesses licensing fees they had owed to music licensing organizations.

The small-establishment exemption shrinks their licensing base and the royalties they collect, but the law preserves their rate-setting power and adds a penalty—double three years' back fees—for establishments that claim the exemption without reasonable grounds.

Twenty extra years of copyright keeps books, films, and recordings locked away from free public use; the new library exemption covers only a work's final 20 years and does not extend to public access.
New termination rights let authors or their estates reclaim copyrights transferred decades earlier, taking rights back from publishers during the extended term.
